content.p: On 13 December 1937 the Japanese army took Nanjing, then the capital of China. Over the next six weeks, soldiers killed Chinese civilians and prisoners, raped women on a very large scale and burned much of the city. How many people died has been disputed ever since. The Tokyo war crimes tribunal put the figure at more than 200,000. China's official figure is 300,000. The Japanese government says only that the killing of a large number of non-combatants took place and that the true number is hard to determine.

Two postwar courts tried officers over what happened. General Matsui Iwane, the commander of the force that took the city, was sentenced to death by hanging in Tokyo for failing to stop the atrocities. Lieutenant General Tani Hisao was tried in Nanjing and sentenced to be shot. The events remain one of the sorest points in relations between China and Japan.

Full-scale war between China and Japan began with the clash at the Marco Polo Bridge on 7 July 1937, according to the USC Shoah Foundation, which dates the earlier Japanese seizure of Manchuria to September 1931. The Japanese army fought its way from Shanghai, about 190 miles down the Yangtze, towards Nanjing. HistoryNet says Japanese troops appeared outside the city walls in November and that fighting raged for weeks.

Chinese leader Chiang Kai-shek concluded that Nanjing was lost. According to History.com, he pulled out nearly all official troops, leaving the city to untrained auxiliary forces, and forbade the official evacuation of civilians. Many fled anyway. HistoryNet describes the Chinese army in the city as disintegrating, with some men surrendering and others discarding their uniforms.

The Japanese troops who arrived were, in History.com's account, hungry, exhausted and undisciplined after weeks of marching and the bloody battle for Shanghai, and many wanted revenge for comrades lost there. HistoryNet adds that the soldiers found themselves outnumbered, short of supplies and holding thousands of prisoners, "a formula for disaster".

As the Japanese approached, a handful of Westerners stayed behind. They formed an international committee that set up a refuge in the northwest of the city, where most foreign embassies and residences stood. History.com dates its opening to November 1937 and compares its area to Central Park in New York, with more than a dozen small camps inside. The nomination file China later submitted to UNESCO says 17 foreigners who stayed in Nanjing set up the committee.

HistoryNet estimates that these businessmen, educators and missionaries shielded about 200,000 people. Its best-known figures are John Rabe, a German Siemens employee elected to lead the zone, who sheltered hundreds in his home, and the teacher and missionary Minnie Vautrin, who turned the Ginling Women's College campus into a refuge for women. The UNESCO file also credits the American missionary John Magee with risking his life to film the atrocities; the footage was developed secretly at Shanghai and smuggled out, and was later shown in Berlin, London and Washington.

The zone did not hold. According to History.com, the Japanese had first agreed to respect it, but even the refugees there were not safe from attacks and killings. The USC Shoah Foundation notes that families living outside it were massacred. In January 1938 the Japanese declared the city subdued and ordered the zone dissolved, and the USC account says that when people went home, the atrocities resumed.

The judgment of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, delivered in November 1948, describes the first weeks. It says that individual soldiers and small groups roamed over the city murdering, raping, looting and burning, that there was "no discipline whatever", and that many soldiers were drunk. It found that at least 12,000 non-combatants were killed in the first two or three days, and it cites another witness as saying that "Chinese were hunted like rabbits, everyone seen to move was shot."

On rape, the judgment gave approximately 20,000 cases inside the city in the first month, with girls and old women among the victims, and many women killed and mutilated afterwards. It said looted shops and homes were frequently set on fire, and that approximately one third of the city was destroyed, with burning that continued for six weeks.

The judges described the mass killing of men as organised. It said it was carried out "with the apparent sanction of the commanders", on the pretext that soldiers had shed their uniforms and mixed with civilians. Groups were bound, marched outside the walls and shot or bayoneted, and more than 20,000 men of military age were known to have died this way. Of the civilians who fled Nanjing, over 57,000 were overtaken and interned, and many of them died. Chinese soldiers who laid down their arms outside the city were, the judgment said, killed within 72 hours by machine gun along the Yangtze, over 30,000 of them, without any pretence of a trial.

From these findings the tribunal arrived at its estimate: over 200,000 civilians and prisoners of war murdered in Nanking and its vicinity in the first six weeks. It said the estimate was not exaggerated, because burial societies and other organisations had counted more than 155,000 bodies they buried, most with their hands tied behind them. It noted that this count did not include bodies burned, thrown into the river or otherwise disposed of.

The judgment also quotes what Japanese diplomats said at the time. On 14 December an embassy official told the Safety Zone committee that the army was "determined to make it bad for Nanking", and that only 17 military policemen had been provided to keep order. Dr Bates testified that the terror was intense for two and a half to three weeks and serious for six to seven weeks, and the committee's secretary, Smythe, filed two protests a day for the first six weeks.
content.h2: Matsui and the question of command
content.p: The tribunal said Matsui stayed in a rear area until 17 December, when he made a triumphal entry, and that he remained in the city for nearly a week. He and his staff officer Muto admitted hearing of the atrocities, and Matsui admitted that foreign governments were protesting, but "no effective action was taken". The judgment records that rape, arson and murder continued for at least six weeks after the city fell and at least four weeks after Matsui and Muto entered. A new garrison commander, General Amaya, was still criticising the foreigners' reports on 5 February 1938.

Following unfavorable reports and pressure of public opinion in nations around the world, the judgment said, Tokyo recalled Matsui together with roughly 80 of his officers, yet none of them was punished, and Matsui was later decorated for "meritorious services" in the China War. In explaining his recall, the judgment says, Matsui said he was not replaced because of the atrocities but because he considered his work ended and wished to retire from the army.

The verdict hinged on a failure to act. According to the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall's own study of the trial, the tribunal convicted Matsui and Hirota Koki, then foreign minister, of neglecting their legal duty to prevent the massacre. That was the only crime Matsui was charged with, and he was sentenced to death by hanging for it. The tribunal did not adopt Count 45, the prosecution's separate charge of murder by the army at Nanjing, and in the end kept only ten counts. The study says this gave later Japanese deniers a pretext, and that the tribunal's own numbers varied: over 200,000 in the general chapter, "upwards of 100,000" in the section on Matsui.

A second proceeding took place in China. Tani Hisao, a lieutenant general, was charged with class B and C war crimes, was extradited to China at the Chinese government's request and stood trial before the Nanjing War Crimes Tribunal. A study of the UNESCO controversy in Frontiers in Political Science says Tani rejected every charge, but the court found him guilty and ordered that he be shot. The nomination file adds that this tribunal concluded that "at least 300,000 Chinese were killed", and that its records include hearings, cross-examinations and defence statements, and that a set of photographs taken from a Japanese officer's film, printed secretly by an apprentice at a Nanjing studio, was listed as important evidence.

The Tokyo tribunal as a whole convicted twenty-five defendants, the USC Shoah Foundation says: seven were hanged, among them Prime Minister Tojo Hideki, sixteen got life terms and two lesser sentences. The Japanese government paroled the prisoners in 1956 and released them unconditionally in 1958.

The figures on offer are: 300,000, China's official number; "over 200,000", the Tokyo judgment; and "upwards of 100,000", the finding on Matsui in the same judgment. The USC Shoah Foundation says as many as 300,000 civilians and unarmed soldiers were killed over two months, and calls a precise count impossible because of the chaos, the fires and the mass graves. History.com says there are no official numbers but gives estimates of 200,000 to 300,000, and puts the number of women raped at between 20,000 and 80,000.

Japan's government accepts that a massacre of non-combatants happened but says the number cannot be verified. Japanese politicians and historians, The Diplomat notes, have publicly claimed the real total was a fraction of 300,000. ABC News reported that some respected foreign academics put the number lower than China does, while "very little mainstream scholarship" doubts a massacre took place. Outside Japan, the Frontiers study says, readings of the events seem to agree that the argument over numbers should not obscure that a very large number died as the army exacted revenge on a population that had stood in its way. In Japan some conservatives and nationalists deny that atrocities occurred, ABC said; it also reported that Japan had rebuffed protests in April 2015 over textbooks that called the events an "incident".
content.h2: Memory, testimony and the UNESCO dispute
content.p: The Memorial Hall in Nanjing was built around a mass grave excavated in the early 1980s, with skeletons left half-buried beside placards describing how the victims died. The Wilson Center says it opened on 15 August 1985; HistoryNet says 1986. It was extended in 1997 for the 60th anniversary, again in 2007, and in December 2015 a Victory Exhibition Hall opened. The Wilson Center argues that the museum's changing emphasis has mirrored the Communist Party's shifting national narrative, from "victor" to "victim" to "rejuvenation".

The USC Shoah Foundation, working with the hall from 2012, recorded 102 testimonies from survivors, in Mandarin, until 2017. By January 2015 the average age of the survivors it had interviewed was 85, and the oldest was 94.

In October 2015 UNESCO inscribed the "Documents of Nanjing Massacre" in its Memory of the World register after a nomination from seven Chinese museums and archives. The collection covers the atrocities themselves, the postwar tribunals and the later trials of Japanese war criminals held in China in the 1950s. China's nomination accused Japan of a "deliberate cover-up of the truth". It also records that Japanese forces burned and buried files shortly before the August 1945 surrender, and that buried remnants found in the 1950s included a military police report on Nanjing from February 1938.

Japan's foreign ministry called the decision "extremely regrettable" and said it would seek reform of the programme so it would not be used politically. The Diplomat quoted chief cabinet secretary Yoshihide Suga calling the decision biased and "problematic", reported Japan's warning that it might stop its UNESCO payments, and said the Yomiuri Shimbun accused China of using a cultural heritage system for political ends. The Frontiers study says Japan did withdraw its UNESCO funding, though it adds, in a note, that another possible factor was a separate proposed listing on "comfort women". It says Japan's funding withdrawal produced promises of reform in the register and that Japan then resumed its payments. The Diplomat's own view was that no major tangible consequences seemed to follow.
